title: Cop31 live: world urged to avoid one of ‘most disappointing Cops ever’ as talks stretch past deadline
text:
Diplomats race to compromise, a full day after the scheduled end
Fiona Harvey
After all the running down corridors, here is where we are:
After marching into the offices of the joint presidencies en masse and with “the whole world” as one participant put it, at about 6.10pm this evening in Turkey, the EU stayed in the meeting with the joint presidencies only briefly, leaving at about 6.30pm, while many developing countries and the UK stayed in.
The UK and the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS) countries remained in the meeting with the presidencies for nearly an hour.
The Guardian understands that the EU left because it needed to have a coordination meeting with its member states and the high ambition coalition, to discuss its way forward.
The issue for the EU is the text under consideration. One possible version would include a reference to the UAE consensus decision at Cop28, paragraph 28 of which contained the key resolution to “transition away from fossil fuels”. This oblique reference to the phaseout of fossil fuels was also the formulation used last year at Belem.
The Guardian understands that such an oblique reference would be acceptable to the High Ambition Coalition, which comprises many developing countries, the UK and some other allies, but there is still a question mark over whether the EU member states will agree to it, or demand something stronger and more explicit.
The EU is now consulting on that.
The Guardian also understands that Saudi Arabia refused to drop its demand for carbon capture and storage (CCS) to be strongly recommended in the text, on a par with the target for electrification, and still refuses to allow any reference to the “transition away from fossil fuels”.
If this standoff continues and if Saudi continues to hold out on CCS and to refuse any references to fossil fuels, the next step – which the Guardian understands is being actively considered by the EU – could be to force a plenary, at which Saudi Arabia would have to either go along with the consensus or publicly oppose the revised wording.
This is a risky strategy, as Saudi Arabia and its allies could hold out. But Bill Hare, chief executive of the Climate Analytics thinktank, and a longtime observer of Cops, told the Guardian it might be the only strategy left. Some believe the Arab Group is no longer as united behind Saudi Arabia as that country had assumed at the outset of these talks.
“If the overwhelming number of countries here want a strong text, referencing the transition away from fossil fuels and so on, and Saudi Arabia is on its own, I think Saudi Arabia will probably not stand against the global consensus,” Hare said.
The three key demands of the countries calling themselves the progressive coalition are now: a reference to the transition away from fossil fuels, or to the UAE Consensus decision in which that resolution appeared; for stronger wording on the tripling of adaptation finance for developing countries; and for any reference to CCS to be either removed or to be weakened and “balanced” by strong language on electrification.
The Guardian also understands that China and India, though not allied with the EU, the UK and the High Ambition Coalition and their allies, who number about 130 countries, are unlikely to stand against those countries.
A predicament “that never should have deteriorated so far” is how Jasper Inventor, head of the Greenpeace’s delegation, has described the current situation at Cop31, as weary delegates bemoan the lack of a new draft deal or clarity over the next steps.
“The fact that no text has been distributed and no actual negotiations between parties has been happening throughout the day is a predicament, and the situation should never have deteriorated so far,” he said. “Parties need to be sitting across the table, looking each other in the eye and negotiating the text themselves, not waiting behind closed doors for the Presidency to produce a compromise.”
He added: “The climate crisis is accelerating beyond the negotiating rooms here in Antalya and yet we are still waiting for a text that aims to address the root cause of the crisis – ending fossil fuels.”
What if too many people go home? Giuliana Viglione, associate editor at Carbon Brief, has explored the prospect of Cop31 being suspended if too many delegates leave to catch flights back to their countries.
If and when delegations start departing the country, the Cop may be in danger of losing quorum.
According to the UNFCCC’s draft rules of procedure, two-thirds of parties must be present in order for decisions to be made. (The US is technically still a party to the convention, so this means 132 out of 198 parties to the UNFCCC – and 130 out of 194 parties to the Paris Agreement.)
A loss of quorum would mean a suspension of the talks, which would have to be resumed at a later date.
While we wait for more from the presidencies, here is an interesting sidelight on this year’s Cop. Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, has been one of the stars of Antalya. His blistering attack on the state of negotiations on Wednesday became a rallying call for “climate-progressive” countries and groups.
The world was “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia”, he told a press conference for the Fossil Fuel Anti-Proliferation Treaty Initiative. “We are in love with our kidnappers. We love the petroleum guys. We can’t live without them, and they are so smart they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.”
But in another set of vital climate-related negotiations, Panama has been playing a markedly different role.
At the International Maritime Organisation, countries are working on a potential levy on the carbon dioxide emitted from international shipping. This levy has been more than a decade in development, as shipping companies and countries reliant on maritime transport have been reluctant for many years to address the 2-3% of global emissions contributed by the industry.
Two years ago, it looked as if green voices had finally won out – IMO members had agreed a framework for cutting their emissions, and a levy on carbon dioxide emissions to help it along. Money raised by the levy – which could amount to tens of billions of dollars a year – could go to help clean up shipping, but some could be diverted to help the most vulnerable countries recover from the impacts of climate catastrophe.
Then came Donald Trump. The US president was bitterly opposed, and members of his administration started a campaign to halt the levy. Some IMO participants described being bullied by the US, while others were threatened with US visa revocation if they did not back down and change their positions.
The campaign worked: at a meeting of the IMO, enough members switched their position to allow for a postponement of the levy.
Next week, at crunch meetings at the IMO headquarters in London, the talks will resume, with a further delay possible. And this time, Panama is on the side of the delayers.
Tristan Smith, professor of energy and transport at University College London, told the Guardian: “Panama’s position moved from supporting the progressive solutions – the levy and the net zero framework [to cut shipping emissions] – in the first half of 2025, to leading the discussion on the weakest alternative to the net zero framework in the first half of 2026.”
Analysis by Smith showed that Panama’s proposals would have produced higher greenhouse gas emissions than alternative plans on the table. Another group of shipping experts told the Guardian they believed there was a “major disconnect” between Panama’s environment ministry and its Maritime and Canal Authority.
As a result, the good work done for the climate at Cop could be undone at the IMO negotiations next week, if shipping interests win out over those who want to cut shipping’s emissions and use a carbon levy to help poor countries stricken by climate disaster.
John Maggs, Coordinator and Accredited Representative to the IMO for the Clean Shipping Coalition, said: “We just hope that the Panamanian delegation that turns up at IMO next week takes heed of what their Environment Ministry is saying and supports adoption of the NZF [Net-Zero Framework].”
The Panama delegation at Cop31 was contacted for comment.
The Cop31 negotiations are an “insult” to people already suffering because of climate breakdown, campaigners have said.
“This must be the last time we allow fossil fuel interests, which are profiting so handsomely from the climate crisis, to hold us to ransom,” said Nick Dearden, director of Global Justice Now, a campaign group. “It is abundantly clear by now that we will not be able to combat climate change as long as those who control the global economy can make money from coal, oil and gas.
The group is calling for a “coalition of the willing” to come together at the second summit to transition away from fossil fuels, which will be co-hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland in 2027.
He added: “After people have experienced the impact of climate change so concretely this summer, it is an insult that a summit supposed to address climate change is struggling to even mention fossil fuels.”

Large crowds gathered outside the entrance to the Cop presidency offices after a group of leaders went in together.
One source connected to the group said it included the Alliance of Small Island States (39 low lying countries), AILAC (Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Honduras, Panama, Peru), the EU, the UK and the grouping of Least Developed Countries.
“Nearly the whole world is in there,” they said.
Two issues the group wanted to raise, the source said, was inclusion of text on the transition away from fossil fuels and to include language around the tripling of finance for climate adaptation that was agreed at Cop29 in Baku.
The EU climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra, and Ireland’s climate minister, Darragh O’Brien, emerged first, sparking a chaotic chasing media pack of cameras (and me) that went out on to the outside walkway and then back inside offices further up.
I asked O’Brien if he was still confident of an agreement being reached. He replied:
Every day throughout Cop, the Climate Action Network, the biggest coalition of climate groups at the summit, hands out an award to the country, individual or body it sees as being most obstructive.
And then, at the end of the two weeks, they hand out the Colossal Fossil award, to the country, individual or body that has most obstructed the course of the summit overall.
This year, as the Antalya climate talks approached their scheduled end, there really could only be one Colossal Fossil. Cop31 itself.
“A colossal waste of time. A colossal distraction. A colossal injustice. And now, a Colossal Fossil,” the group said in an email announcing the award.
“This award is not for the negotiators, communities and civil society who fought day and night in good faith for agreements that protect lives, nor for the venue workers who have fed, accommodated and looked after us with such patience and warmth.
“It goes to those who made sure those agreements were never delivered.”
And who were they? Well, according to CAN, they were:
the developed countries, who “spent two weeks resisting finance commitments and demonstrating how efficiently international cooperation can be brought to a grinding halt”;
the lobbyists, a record 700 of whom stalked the halls of Cop31 Antalya, according to CAN, turning the climate summit into “a trade fair for the people causing the problem”;
and the presidencies, Turkey and Australia, who “fought for the privilege of leading Cop31, then dropped the ball when the world needed them most”.
CAN noted that on Thursday, Murat Kurum had said Cop31 was shaping up to be “the best Cop ever”.
“Congratulations, Cop31. You promised to be the Implementation COP, and instead you’ve implemented a masterclass in obstruction. The best COP ever? You’ve certainly been the best at being the worst.”
Will there be a walkout? Will the talks break down? Let’s look back at some Cops of the past.
2000: The negotiators at Cop6, held in The Hague, could not resolve their disagreements. In the closing plenary, the host Jan Pronk suspended the talks, expressing his disappointment and admitting that the expectations of the “outside world” had not been met. The talks were reconvened eight months later at a special meeting.
2009: The best-known climate summit disaster was at Cop15 in Copenhagen. After intense international buildup, and huge backlash from developing countries over the handling of the talks, the original Cop president was sidelined and the Danish prime minister stepped in to take over. The conference worked its way through eight draft texts, but talks collapsed and negotiations ended with the weak Copenhagen accord, which recognised that climate change was one of the great challenges of our time. The deal was just “taken note of” rather than “adopted”. Still, developing countries agreed to curb future emissions growth for the first time, and the commitments on emissions cuts made there by both developed and developing countries at the summit were largely achieved and on deadline.
2013: Representatives of most of the world’s poor countries walked out after developed countries sought to delay discussion over compensation for extreme climate events. They eventually returned, resulting in the creation of the Warsaw internationsal mechanism for loss and damage.
2021: Although Cop26 at Glasgow got an agreement in the end, it took many hours of negotiation and involved a last-minute intervention by India to water down language on “phasing out” coal to merely “phasing down”, a concession which left Cop host Alok Sharma visibly emotional.
2024: At Cop28 in Baku, two major sub-blocs of the G77 – the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS) and the Least Developed Countries (LDCs) – walked out of overtime climate finance talks in protest of an initial $250bn annual funding offer from wealthy nations, which they called inadequate and unconsulted; both groups subsequently returned to the talks. From the beginning the Baku presidency said they would have no cover text, which was controversial. As Carbon Brief put it: “Some observers expressed relief at the decision, while others questioned the can of worms that would have been opened if a cover-text negotiation had been started.”
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK energy minister and head of the UK delegation, marched to the presidency offices today at 6.08pm local time with some EU ministers and heads of delegation from a number of small islands and developing countries, including Fiji’s minister and Ralph Regenvanu of Vanuatu.
About 30 to 40 countries made up the group. The Guardian understands they went to call on the presidency not to backslide from the commitments made previously on fossil fuels, to include a tripling of adaptation finance for developing countries, and for any reference to CCS to be “balanced” by targets on electrification.
Cop31 President Murat Kurum has called on every country to act responsibly. “Getting bogged down in individual words and expressions and undermining this process serves noone’s interests,” he said in comments reported by AFP.
The words in question are presumably fossil fuels, which were stripped from the draft deal earlier this week.
As Cop31 drags deeper into overtime and negotiators fiddle with brackets and adverbs, out in the real world the impacts of climate change are already hitting.
Both US coasts have been facing huge tidal surges and flooding for the last couple of weeks. It’s partly due to the “godzilla” El Niño that is coming through this year which has been closely connected to global heating. But climate change and the resulting sea level rise has also made the usual ‘king tides’ far stronger, as meteorologist, oceanographer and CEO of Brizaga Alec Bogdanoff explained earlier this month:
Climate change is a force multiplier. So what’s happening, at least for sea level rise, is it’s heating our oceans. So you can think of it like an old mercury thermometer. The oceans are expanding as they warm.”
In Florida heavy rains have further worsened the problems.
Now the mayor of San Francisco, Daniel Lurie, is warning that next week the city faces a possible emergency.
We are anticipating high tides and rain that this city has never seen before. This is extremely serious, and we are acting accordingly at the city level. We are going to encourage every resident and business owner to take this extremely seriously. We are standing up our Emergency Operations Center late this weekend. Our crews are out now and will be every single day going forward.”
Countries in East and South Africa have also been hit by torrential rains connected to El Niño. At least 12 are reported dead in floods in Kenya; in Soweto, South African searchers found the body of an 11-year-old who had been swept away by flash floods a couple of days earlier.
On current trends, 2026 is likely to tie with 2024 as the hottest year in recorded history, according to Zeke Hausfather, writing in Carbon Brief.
My colleague Jonathan Watts explored some of the extraordinary weather events that this year has brought here:
Most countries back push to mention fossil fuels in deal, EU believes
Fiona Harvey
The Guardian understands that the EU believes it has 130 countries allied behind its push to get a mention of fossil fuels, and the need to move away from them, into the final text.
This number includes scores of developing countries, including some of the poorest and most vulnerable countries bearing the brunt of climate damage.
As Graham notes below, the Guardian also understands that the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has not yet made any phone calls to his counterparts in capitals around the world, to try to break the impasse. The heads of delegation at Cop31 are mostly at the ministerial level, usually environment, climate or energy ministers, and many would require new instructions from their capitals to shift from their entrenched negotiating positions.
At late stages of previous Cops, there have been calls made between the country leaders and other heads of state in an attempt to break through disagreements.
We have confirmed that, as far as the Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese is concerned, there have not been any calls from him yet to his counterparts.
Consensus-driven talks to forge a global treaty with potentially existential consequences for humanity collapsed on Saturday morning. No, not the Cop31 climate summit – we’re still waiting for that outcome. These were UN talks to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons.
Russia led objections with obstructive stalling tactics, while other countries who have invested heavily in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other such weapons. Among the military powers who wanted only a nonbinding agreement were the UK, France, Germany, South Korea, Japan and Turkey.
The main sticking point now is countries, including the EU, small islands and other vulnerable developing nations, trying to get a reference to fossil fuels and the need to transition away from them reinserted in some form into the text. The Guardian has been unable to establish whether the heads of state of the joint presidencies – Recep Tayyip Erdoğan of Turkey and Anthony Albanese of Australia – have made phone calls to their counterparts in foreign capitals, to try to break the impasse.
Pelin Zorlu, senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, told the Guardian: “Erdoğan or Hakan Fidan, Turkey’s foreign minister, calling Saudi will be absolutely necessary to unblock this. Otherwise, there is an increasing probability that Turkey will take the diplomatic blame, as the country that will gavel it through.”
